Indexation increases are always charged at smoker rates
The extra cover is usually priced at his age when the increase is applied, so it costs more per euro than his original cover
Indexation removes the guarantee on the original premium
questions.explanation: Typically each increase in cover is charged at rates for the life assured's age at the time of the increase. Because he is older, the extra cover costs more per euro than the original cover.

questions.question: Orla, 32, has level term cover with a guaranteed insurability option. She has just had her first child. What does the option typically allow her to do?
options: Increase her cover within set limits without providing further medical evidence
Reduce her premium because she now has a dependant
Add her child as a joint life assured
Cash in part of the policy to pay childcare costs
questions.explanation: A guaranteed insurability option lets the policyholder increase cover on specified life events, such as the birth of a child, marriage or a larger mortgage, within limits and without new medical underwriting.

questions.question: All other factors being equal, which applicant will usually pay the highest premium for level term cover?
options: A 30-year-old non-smoker in good health
A 30-year-old smoker in good health
A 45-year-old non-smoker in good health
A 45-year-old smoker in good health
questions.explanation: Mortality risk increases with age and smoking, so the older smoker presents the highest risk and pays the highest premium.

questions.question: Which of the following may an insurer NOT use as a factor in setting individual life assurance premiums in Ireland for new policies?
options: The applicant's age
Whether the applicant smokes
The applicant's gender
The policy term and sum assured
questions.explanation: Since 21 December 2012, following the Test-Achats ruling of the Court of Justice of the EU, insurers cannot use gender as a factor that results in different individual premiums and benefits. Age, smoker status, health, term and sum assured remain key factors.

questions.question: What does waiver of premium benefit provide?
options: A refund of all premiums if no claim is made
Payment of the policy's premiums by the insurer if the policyholder cannot work due to illness or injury, after a deferred period
A lump sum if the life assured is diagnosed with a specified illness
A reduction in premium for non-smokers
questions.explanation: Waiver of premium keeps the policy in force by having the insurer pay the premiums while the insured is unable to work through illness or injury, once the deferred period has passed.

questions.question: Brian earns €60,000 a year and has a €250,000 mortgage (with no mortgage protection) and an employer death-in-service benefit of €200,000. His spouse needs €42,000 a year for 20 years if he dies. Ignoring investment returns, inflation and State benefits, how much additional life cover does he need?
questions.explanation: Income need: €42,000 x 20 = €840,000. Add the mortgage: €840,000 + €250,000 = €1,090,000. Deduct existing cover: €1,090,000 - €200,000 = €890,000. €1,090,000 ignores existing cover, €640,000 omits the mortgage and €1,250,000 uses his full salary.
questions.reference: Quantifying the need for life cover

questions.question: When quantifying a client's need for life cover, how should an existing death-in-service benefit from the client's employer be treated?
options: It should be ignored because it is not a personal policy
It can be deducted from the need, but the adviser should note it is likely to end if the client changes or leaves employment
It should be added to the need because it is taxable
It should be deducted, and it will continue for life once the client has joined the scheme
questions.explanation: Existing cover reduces the shortfall, but death-in-service benefit is tied to employment and usually ends when the client leaves that employer, so relying on it fully carries a risk.

questions.question: In a needs analysis for a married client with young children, how should State benefits that the surviving spouse may receive (such as a widow's, widower's or surviving civil partner's pension) be treated?
options: They should be ignored entirely because they are always too small to matter
They should be assumed to replace the client's full income
They can be taken into account in outline as a source of income, with life cover arranged for the remaining shortfall
They should be added to the sum assured needed
questions.explanation: State benefits can partly meet the family's income need, so a needs analysis may allow for them, subject to eligibility, and recommend cover for the shortfall. They will rarely replace a full salary.

questions.question: Liam is 26, single, has no dependants and no debts, and is renting. He relies entirely on his salary. Which protection need is likely to be his highest priority?
options: Large amounts of level term life cover
Income protection in case he cannot work through illness
Joint life first death whole of life cover
Family income benefit
questions.explanation: With no dependants or debts, little financial loss would result from his death, but losing his income through illness would affect him directly. Income protection is therefore the more relevant priority.

questions.question: Joan, 40, needs €300,000 of cover until her children are independent in 20 years. Why is term assurance generally more cost-effective for this need than whole of life cover?
options: Because term assurance pays out on any death, at any age
Because term assurance builds up a surrender value
Because term cover only pays if death occurs within the term, so the insurer is much less likely to pay a claim
Because whole of life cover has a maximum term of 20 years
questions.explanation: Term cover pays only if death occurs within the term, which for a 40-year-old over 20 years is relatively unlikely, so premiums are low. Whole of life cover will certainly pay out eventually and is priced accordingly.

questions.question: Which client need is best met by whole of life cover rather than term assurance?
options: Providing a lump sum on death whenever it occurs, for example to fund an expected inheritance tax liability
Repaying a 25-year repayment mortgage
Replacing income until the youngest child reaches 21
Covering a 5-year business loan
questions.explanation: Needs that exist whenever death occurs, such as funding a future inheritance tax (CAT) bill for beneficiaries, require cover that lasts for life. Debts and needs with a known end date are met more cheaply by term cover.
questions.reference: Term vs whole of life - purpose

questions.question: Which is a key reason why the sale of life assurance products is closely regulated?
options: Life policies are short-term contracts that are easy to cancel
Insurers always know less about the product than consumers do
Consumers often have less information and expertise than providers, and contracts are long-term, so poor advice may only become apparent years later
Regulation guarantees that every policy will produce a profit for the consumer
questions.explanation: Information asymmetry and the long-term, complex nature of life contracts mean consumers rely heavily on advice. Regulation aims to protect consumers and maintain confidence; it does not guarantee investment outcomes.

questions.question: Which body authorises and supervises life assurance companies and insurance intermediaries in Ireland and sets the Consumer Protection Code?
options: The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
The Department of Finance
Revenue
The Central Bank of Ireland
questions.explanation: The Central Bank is responsible for both prudential supervision and conduct of business regulation, including the Consumer Protection Code and Minimum Competency Code. The FSPO resolves individual complaints.
questions.reference: Role of the Central Bank of Ireland

questions.question: Under the Solvency II framework that governs the authorisation and supervision of life assurance undertakings, what does Pillar 1 deal with?
options: Quantitative requirements, such as the valuation of technical provisions and the Solvency Capital Requirement
Governance, risk management and supervisory review
Public disclosure and regulatory reporting
Sales practices and consumer information
questions.explanation: Solvency II has three pillars: Pillar 1 covers quantitative capital requirements (technical provisions, SCR and MCR), Pillar 2 governance and supervisory review, and Pillar 3 reporting and disclosure. Sales conduct is covered by IDD and conduct rules.

questions.question: Under Solvency II, what is the significance of an insurer's own funds falling below its Minimum Capital Requirement (MCR)?
options: It is a routine event requiring no supervisory action
It is the level at which the insurer must stop paying commission
It is the threshold below which policyholders would be exposed to an unacceptable level of risk, and it can lead to withdrawal of authorisation
It means the insurer must transfer all policies to the Insurance Compensation Fund
questions.explanation: The MCR is the lower capital threshold; breaching it triggers the strongest supervisory intervention, ultimately withdrawal of authorisation. Breaching the higher SCR requires a recovery plan.

questions.question: A life insurer authorised in another EEA state sells policies in Ireland on a freedom-of-services basis. Which statement is correct?
options: It must obtain a separate full Irish authorisation before selling any policy
Its prudential (solvency) supervision is carried out by its home state regulator, while Irish conduct of business rules can apply to its Irish business
It is not subject to any Irish rules at all
Its Irish policies are covered by the Insurance Compensation Fund instead of its home regulator's supervision
questions.explanation: Under EU passporting, the home state supervises solvency, while the host state (Ireland) can apply certain conduct rules to protect local consumers. The Insurance Compensation Fund does not cover life policies.

questions.question: Which legislation currently governs the registration of insurance intermediaries, including those advising on life assurance, in Ireland?
options: The European Union (Insurance Distribution) Regulations 2018, implementing the Insurance Distribution Directive
The Investment Intermediaries Act 1995 only
MiFID II
The Credit Union Act 1997
questions.explanation: Insurance and reinsurance intermediaries are registered with the Central Bank under the Insurance Distribution Regulations 2018 (S.I. 229 of 2018), which transposed the IDD. Life policies are not MiFID instruments.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Protection Code, when may an intermediary describe itself as a 'broker'?
options: When it holds agencies with at least two insurers
When it has been registered for more than five years
When it charges a fee instead of commission
When it provides its services on the basis of a fair analysis of the market
questions.explanation: The 'broker' title is reserved for firms that base their services on a fair analysis of the market (a sufficiently large number of products and providers). Simply holding two agencies does not meet that test.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code: use of the term broker

questions.question: Under the IDD framework, who bears responsibility for the distribution activities of a tied insurance intermediary?
options: The consumer, who chose to deal with a tied agent
The insurance undertaking(s) on whose behalf the tied intermediary acts
The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
No one, as tied intermediaries are unregulated
questions.explanation: A tied insurance intermediary acts under the full responsibility of the insurer(s) it represents, which is why it does not need the same independent registration requirements as a broker.

questions.question: To whom does the Central Bank's Minimum Competency Code principally apply?
options: Only to the boards of directors of life companies
Only to claims handlers in non-life insurers
Staff of regulated firms who provide advice on, or arrange, retail financial products such as life assurance for consumers, and those in certain specified roles
All consumers who buy financial products
questions.explanation: The MCC sets minimum knowledge and competence standards for individuals who advise on or arrange retail financial products (including life assurance) or carry out certain specified functions, such as supervising those who do.

questions.question: Under the Minimum Competency Code, what is the minimum annual continuing professional development (CPD) requirement for accredited persons?
options: 15 hours
5 hours
30 hours
No CPD is required once a qualification is obtained
questions.explanation: Individuals relying on a recognised qualification must complete at least 15 hours of CPD each year to remain competent; the IDD also requires at least 15 hours of training a year for insurance distributors.

questions.question: Darren has joined a broker and wants to give advice on life assurance savings policies to consumers. What does the Minimum Competency Code require of him?
options: Only that he is over 21 and has a clean credit history
That he passes the Central Bank's own entrance examination
That he has five years' experience in banking
That he obtains a recognised qualification appropriate to the product category, such as the QFA, and maintains competence through CPD
questions.explanation: The MCC lists recognised qualifications for each retail product category, and individuals must hold an appropriate one (subject to the Code's transitional supervision arrangements for new staff) and then complete annual CPD.

questions.question: Before recommending a single-premium investment bond, which information must an adviser gather as part of knowing the consumer?
options: Only the amount the client wishes to invest
The client's needs and objectives, personal and financial circumstances, time horizon, attitude to risk and capacity for loss
Only the client's preferred fund manager
The client's PPS number and nothing else
questions.explanation: Suitability depends on a full fact-find: objectives, circumstances, financial situation, investment horizon, risk attitude and ability to absorb losses. Without these, a recommendation cannot be shown to be suitable.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code: knowing the consumer

questions.question: What is a statement of suitability?
options: A document from the insurer confirming the medical underwriting decision
The policy schedule showing the sum assured
A written explanation, given to the consumer before the contract is concluded, of why the recommended product is considered suitable for their needs and circumstances
A form the consumer signs to waive the cooling-off period
questions.explanation: The adviser must document the basis for the recommendation, linking the product to the consumer's needs, objectives and circumstances, and give it to the consumer before the sale, keeping a copy on file.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code: statement of suitability

questions.question: An adviser proposes that a client replace an existing life policy with a new one. What should the adviser do?
options: Inform the client in writing of the potential financial consequences, such as new charges, loss of benefits or re-underwriting, and be satisfied the replacement is in the client's best interests
Arrange the replacement without comment, as the client has the right to cancel during cooling-off
Cancel the old policy first so that the client is not paying for two policies
Avoid mentioning the old policy, as it was sold by a different firm
questions.explanation: Policy replacement can harm consumers through new initial charges, lost guarantees or less favourable underwriting, so the consequences must be explained in writing and the switch must be justified as being in the consumer's interest.
questions.reference: Consumer Protection Code: replacement of policies

questions.question: Gemma, 45, has a mortgage protection policy taken out ten years ago with standard rates. She was recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. She has seen a cheaper new policy advertised and wants to switch. What is the most important advice to give her?
options: She should cancel the existing policy now to save premiums while the new application is processed
She should not cancel the existing cover until any new policy has been accepted on known terms, because new underwriting may result in loadings or exclusions
Her new policy will automatically be issued on her old terms
She does not need to disclose the diagnosis, because it occurred after the original policy started
questions.explanation: The existing policy was underwritten on her health ten years ago. A new application will be underwritten on her current health, so the new cover could cost more or exclude conditions; she must disclose the diagnosis on any new application.

questions.question: What does the Consumer Protection Code expect of firms dealing with consumers who may be in vulnerable circumstances, for example after a bereavement or a serious diagnosis?
options: Firms should refuse to deal with them until their circumstances improve
Firms must always obtain a court order before selling them a policy
Firms should treat them exactly the same as all other consumers, with no adjustments
Firms should identify such consumers and provide reasonable arrangements or assistance to help them in their dealings with the firm
questions.explanation: The Code requires firms to recognise vulnerability and adapt their approach (for example more time, clearer information or allowing a trusted person to help). The revised Code applying from 24 March 2026 strengthened the focus on consumers in vulnerable circumstances.

questions.question: Under the Life Assurance (Provision of Information) Regulations 2001, which of the following must be disclosed to a prospective policyholder before a policy is taken out?
options: The insurer's internal underwriting manual
The adviser's personal income for the previous year
Details of the intermediary's or sales remuneration, along with projected benefits and charges
The names of other clients who bought the same policy
questions.explanation: The 2001 Regulations require pre-contract information including illustrations of benefits, the effect of charges, and the remuneration payable to the intermediary or salesperson, so the consumer can compare products.

questions.question: A consumer is unhappy with a life company's final response to her complaint about a claim. To which body can she refer the complaint?
options: The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman
The Insurance Compensation Fund
The Data Protection Commission
The Competition and Consumer Protection Commission
questions.explanation: Once the firm's internal complaints process is exhausted, the consumer can bring the complaint to the FSPO, which provides an independent, free dispute resolution service for financial services complaints.

questions.question: What is the status of a legally binding decision issued by the Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman?
options: It is a recommendation the firm may ignore
It is binding on the consumer only
It is binding on both parties, subject to a right of appeal to the High Court
It can only be enforced if the Central Bank agrees
questions.explanation: FSPO legally binding decisions bind both the complainant and the provider, who may appeal to the High Court. The service is free to consumers.

questions.question: Why is it essential for an adviser to keep complete records of the fact-find and the reasons for a recommendation?
options: So that the records can be sold to other firms for marketing
To show that the advice was suitable, which may be needed if the consumer complains or the Central Bank reviews the file
Because the insurer will refuse claims without them
Because records replace the need to give the client a statement of suitability
questions.explanation: The Code requires firms to keep records that demonstrate compliance, including the information gathered and the basis for advice. In a complaint or inspection, undocumented advice is hard to defend.

questions.question: For how long does a consumer who takes out an individual life assurance policy in Ireland have the right to cancel it under the cooling-off rules?
options: 7 days
14 days
60 days
30 days
questions.explanation: Life assurance policyholders have a 30-day cooling-off period, running from when they are informed that the contract has been concluded, during which they can cancel the policy.

questions.question: From when does the cooling-off period for an individual life assurance policy generally run?
options: From the date the consumer first meets the adviser
From the date the consumer is informed that the contract has been concluded
From the first anniversary of the policy
From the date of the first claim
questions.explanation: The period starts when the policyholder is told that the policy is in force (for example on receipt of the policy documents/notification), so they can review the final terms before deciding.

questions.question: Under the Insurance Distribution Regulations, what must be identified and documented before any insurance contract, including a life policy, is concluded?
options: The consumer's demands and needs
The consumer's credit score
The insurer's Solvency II ratio
The adviser's examination results
questions.explanation: Every insurance distributor must specify the customer's demands and needs and ensure that any contract proposed is consistent with them, whether or not advice is given.

questions.question: Which standardised pre-contract document must be provided to a retail investor before they invest in a unit-linked life assurance bond?
options: An Insurance Product Information Document (IPID)
A MiFID prospectus
A Key Information Document (KID) under the PRIIPs Regulation
A Solvency and Financial Condition Report
questions.explanation: Unit-linked bonds are insurance-based investment products (IBIPs) and so are PRIIPs requiring a KID. The IPID applies to non-life insurance products.

questions.question: The Insurance Product Information Document (IPID) required under the IDD applies to which type of product?
options: Insurance-based investment products
Occupational pension schemes
Term assurance and whole-of-life policies
Non-life insurance products
questions.explanation: The IPID is a standardised summary for non-life products such as motor or home insurance. IBIPs use the PRIIPs KID, and other life products are covered by life-specific information rules.

questions.question: Under the IDD, what must an insurance intermediary disclose to a customer about its remuneration before a contract is concluded?
options: The nature of the remuneration it receives, for example a fee, commission, other remuneration or a combination
Nothing, as remuneration is a confidential commercial matter
Only the remuneration of the insurer's directors
Its total annual profit for the previous year
questions.explanation: The IDD requires disclosure of the nature of remuneration in connection with the contract, and in some cases further detail (for example for IBIPs, information on costs and charges including distribution costs).

questions.question: When an intermediary gives advice on an insurance-based investment product under the IDD, which assessment must it carry out?
options: Only a check that the customer is resident in the EEA
A suitability assessment covering the customer's knowledge and experience, financial situation including ability to bear losses, and investment objectives including risk tolerance
A medical assessment of the life assured
An appropriateness test only, without regard to objectives
questions.explanation: For advised IBIP sales, the IDD requires a suitability assessment of knowledge and experience, financial situation (including capacity for loss) and objectives (including risk tolerance), with a suitability statement for the customer.

questions.question: Why are unit-linked life assurance bonds sold in Ireland not regulated under MiFID II?
options: Because they carry no investment risk
Because they are regulated only by Revenue
Because they are not financial instruments under MiFID; insurance-based investment products are governed by the IDD and the PRIIPs Regulation
Because MiFID II applies only to bank deposits
questions.explanation: Life assurance contracts are insurance, not MiFID financial instruments. The IDD extended MiFID-style conduct protections (suitability, conflicts, costs disclosure) to IBIPs, and PRIIPs requires the KID.
questions.reference: MiFID II scope; IDD and PRIIPs

questions.question: Under the GDPR, how is information about an applicant's health collected for life assurance underwriting classified?
options: Public data
Anonymous data
Ordinary contact data
Special category personal data
questions.explanation: Data concerning health is special category data under Article 9 GDPR, which may only be processed where a specific condition applies in addition to a lawful basis.

questions.question: What does a life insurer need in order to lawfully process an applicant's health data for underwriting?
options: Nothing, because the applicant chose to apply
A lawful basis under Article 6 GDPR and a separate condition under Article 9, such as the applicant's explicit consent
Only the intermediary's verbal confirmation
Approval from the Central Bank for each application
questions.explanation: Processing special category data requires both a general lawful basis and an Article 9 condition. Explicit consent is commonly relied on for obtaining medical information, such as a GP report, during underwriting.

questions.question: In underwriting a life policy in Ireland, which of the following is an insurer prohibited by law from requesting or using?
options: The results of a genetic test
A report from the applicant's GP, with consent
The applicant's smoking status
The applicant's height and weight
questions.explanation: The Disability Act 2005 prohibits insurers from requesting, processing or using the results of genetic tests. GP reports may be obtained with the applicant's consent, and lifestyle and build information is routinely used.

questions.question: A policyholder makes a data subject access request to her life insurer under the GDPR. Within what period must the insurer normally respond?
options: Five working days
Six months
One month, extendable in certain circumstances
One year
questions.explanation: Under Article 12 GDPR, the controller must respond without undue delay and within one month, which can be extended by two further months for complex or numerous requests.

questions.question: Under the Criminal Justice (Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing) Act 2010, what must a life company or intermediary normally do before establishing a business relationship with a customer?
options: Obtain the customer's tax clearance certificate
Obtain a credit reference
Report the customer to An Garda Síochána
Carry out customer due diligence, including identifying the customer and verifying their identity
questions.explanation: Designated persons, including life insurers and insurance intermediaries, must apply customer due diligence, verifying identity on a risk-based approach, before entering into a business relationship.

questions.question: A new client invests €400,000 in a single-premium bond, paid from an overseas account, and asks to cancel it within the cooling-off period, with the refund paid to a different third-party account. Why is this a money-laundering concern?
options: Single-premium bonds are illegal for non-residents
Cancellation can be used to obtain apparently clean funds from a reputable insurer, and paying a third party obscures the money trail
The client will have to pay exit tax on the refund
Cancelling within cooling-off is not permitted for single-premium bonds
questions.explanation: Large single premiums followed by early cancellation and refunds to third parties are classic laundering indicators. The firm should apply enhanced scrutiny and consider a suspicious transaction report.
questions.reference: AML risk in single-premium life business

questions.question: To whom must a designated person in Ireland report a suspicion of money laundering?
options: The Financial Services and Pensions Ombudsman and the Central Bank
The customer's bank and the insurer's auditors
FIU Ireland (An Garda Síochána) and the Revenue Commissioners
The Data Protection Commission
questions.explanation: Suspicious transaction reports go to the Financial Intelligence Unit of An Garda Síochána and to Revenue, normally via the firm's money laundering reporting officer.

questions.question: Having made a suspicious transaction report about a client, an adviser is asked by the client why the bond application is taking so long. What must the adviser avoid doing?
options: Telling the client anything that discloses that a report has been made or that an investigation may be under way
Responding to the client at all, under any circumstances
Keeping a record of the client's query
Continuing to apply customer due diligence
questions.explanation: Disclosing that a report has been made, or information likely to prejudice an investigation, is the offence of tipping off. The adviser can respond in neutral terms and should consult the MLRO.

questions.question: If an Irish life assurance company were to go into liquidation, would the Insurance Compensation Fund cover its life assurance policyholders?
options: Yes, it pays 100% of all life policy values
Yes, but only for unit-linked policies
Yes, up to €100,000 per policyholder
No, the Insurance Compensation Fund covers non-life insurance, not life assurance
questions.explanation: The Insurance Compensation Fund supports non-life policyholders of insolvent insurers. Life policyholders rely instead on prudential supervision and Solvency II requirements; €100,000 is the deposit guarantee limit for bank deposits.

questions.question: Under a unit-linked savings or investment policy, how is the value of the policyholder's benefit normally determined?
options: The number of units allocated to the policy multiplied by the current unit (bid) price
A guaranteed sum assured plus any reversionary bonuses declared
The total premiums paid plus a fixed rate of interest set at the outset
A bonus rate declared each year by the life company's board
questions.explanation: Premiums buy units in a fund, and the policy value at any time is the number of units held times the current unit price. The policyholder bears the investment risk; guaranteed sums and declared bonuses are features of with-profits contracts.

questions.question: Under a dual-pricing system for unit-linked funds, at which price does a policyholder buy units when a premium is invested?
options: Bid price
Cancellation price
Offer price
Encashment value
questions.explanation: Units are bought at the higher offer price and sold (encashed) at the lower bid price. The difference is the bid/offer spread, which is a charge to the investor.

questions.question: Ciara invests €10,000 in a unit-linked bond with 100% allocation. The fund's offer price is €2.50 and its bid price is €2.375 (a 5% bid/offer spread). How many units are allocated to her policy?
options: 3,800 units
4,200 units
4,000 units
questions.explanation: Units are bought at the offer price: €10,000 ÷ €2.50 = 4,000 units. Dividing by the bid price (giving 4,210.53) is the common mistake; the spread shows up as the immediate drop in value to 4,000 × €2.375 = €9,500.

questions.question: Declan invests a single premium of €50,000 in a unit-linked bond with an allocation rate of 101% and a 5% bid/offer spread. Ignoring any other charges and taxes, what is the bid value of his units immediately after investment?
questions.explanation: Allocated amount = €50,000 × 101% = €50,500; the spread then reduces the bid value by 5%: €50,500 × 0.95 = €47,975. €48,000 wrongly nets the percentages (101% − 5% = 96%), and €47,500 ignores the extra allocation.

questions.question: A regular-premium savings plan has a premium of €100 a month. A policy fee of €4 a month is deducted first, and 98% of the balance is then allocated to units. Assuming no bid/offer spread, how much is invested in units each month?
questions.explanation: The fee comes off first: €100 − €4 = €96; then 98% is allocated: €96 × 0.98 = €94.08. €94.00 results from applying the allocation to the full premium and then deducting the fee (€98 − €4), which is not the order stated.

questions.question: Niamh pays €200 a month into a regular-premium savings plan. In the first year the allocation rate is 95% and there are no other charges. What total amount is allocated to units in the first year (ignoring investment growth)?
questions.explanation: Annual premiums are €200 × 12 = €2,400, and 95% is allocated: €2,400 × 0.95 = €2,280 (€190 a month).

questions.question: A unit-linked fund is worth €100,000 at the start of the year and achieves growth of 6% before charges. The annual management charge is 1.5% of the fund value, deducted at the end of the year. Ignoring tax and other charges, what is the fund value at the end of the year after the AMC?
questions.explanation: End value before AMC = €100,000 × 1.06 = €106,000; AMC = 1.5% × €106,000 = €1,590; net value = €104,410. Simply subtracting 1.5% from the 6% growth rate gives €104,500, which ignores that the charge is levied on the grown fund.

questions.question: Two years after investing €100,000 in a bond, Paul's policy is worth €108,000. If he surrenders now, an early encashment charge of 3% of the policy value applies. What is the surrender value before any exit tax?
questions.explanation: The charge is 3% of the current value: €108,000 × 3% = €3,240, leaving €104,760. Applying 3% to the original premium (€3,000) gives €105,000, which is not how the charge was stated.

questions.question: Which feature is a particular advantage of a regular-premium savings plan compared with a single-premium investment bond?
options: The investor needs a large lump sum at outset to start the plan
Buying units at regular intervals gives the benefit of euro-cost averaging
The policy value is guaranteed not to fall below premiums paid
Gains on regular-premium plans are exempt from exit tax
questions.explanation: Investing a fixed amount each month buys more units when prices are low and fewer when high (euro-cost averaging), which reduces the risk of investing everything at a market peak. Regular-premium plans are still subject to exit tax and carry no capital guarantee unless specifically provided.

questions.question: A single-premium bond advertises a 102% allocation rate. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The extra 2% is a guaranteed return paid by the insurer at maturity
The extra 2% is a tax credit from Revenue on the premium
The encashment value can never fall below 102% of the premium
The insurer usually recoups the extra allocation through other charges, such as a higher AMC or early encashment penalties
questions.explanation: Allocations above 100% are not free money; the cost is recovered through ongoing charges and/or exit penalties if the bond is cashed in during the early years. Unit values can still fall with the market.

questions.question: How is the annual management charge (AMC) on a unit-linked fund usually collected?
options: It is deducted from the fund regularly, so it is reflected in the unit price or taken by cancelling units
It is invoiced to the policyholder each year and paid by separate direct debit
It is deducted only once, from the final proceeds at maturity
It is collected by Revenue together with the life assurance levy
questions.explanation: The AMC is taken from the fund on an ongoing basis (for example daily or monthly), either through the unit price or by cancelling units, so the policyholder does not pay it separately.

questions.question: What is the main reason a life company applies early encashment charges in the first few years of an investment bond?
options: To discourage switching between funds within the bond
To recover set-up costs, such as commission paid to the intermediary, if the policy is cashed in early
To pay the exit tax due to Revenue on surrender
To fund the Insurance Compensation Fund
questions.explanation: Insurers incur most of their costs, notably initial commission, at the start; exit penalties that reduce over time allow them to recover those costs when the policy does not stay in force long enough to recoup them through ongoing charges.

questions.question: Which of the following unit-linked funds would normally carry the lowest risk of capital loss?
options: Global equity fund
Property fund
Emerging markets equity fund
Cash fund
questions.explanation: A cash fund invests in deposits and short-term money market instruments, so its value is relatively stable, although returns may not keep pace with inflation and charges can exceed interest earned.

questions.question: The Key Information Document for an insurance-based investment product shows a summary risk indicator. On what scale is this indicator expressed?
options: 1 to 5
1 to 10
1 to 7
A to G
questions.explanation: Under the PRIIPs Regulation, the KID's summary risk indicator runs from 1 (lowest risk) to 7 (highest risk), combining market risk and credit risk.

questions.question: Eoin holds a unit-linked bond and wants to move his money from an equity fund to a cash fund offered within the same policy. Which statement is correct?
options: The switch is a chargeable event, so exit tax is deducted on any gain
Switching between funds within the policy is normally permitted and is not a chargeable event for exit tax
Switching is only permitted on the eighth anniversary of the policy
He must surrender the bond and take out a new policy to change funds
questions.explanation: Switching between funds inside the same life policy does not involve a disposal of the policy, so no exit tax arises; insurers commonly allow a number of free switches each year.

questions.question: Which risk is particularly associated with a direct property fund in a unit-linked policy?
options: The insurer may be able to defer encashments or switches out of the fund for a period if many investors want to withdraw at once
The fund's value is fixed and cannot rise with property prices
Property funds are not permitted to charge an AMC
Gains in property funds are subject to CGT instead of exit tax
questions.explanation: Property is illiquid and buildings cannot be sold quickly, so policy conditions usually allow the insurer to delay withdrawals from a property fund for a period. Investors in such funds face liquidity risk as well as market risk.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a reversionary bonus on a traditional with-profits policy?
options: A bonus calculated only at maturity based on final investment performance
A bonus the insurer can remove at any time if markets fall
A cash dividend paid out to the policyholder each year
A bonus added to the policy, usually annually, which once added cannot normally be taken away for claims on death or maturity
questions.explanation: Reversionary (annual) bonuses are added to the guaranteed benefits and, once declared, become guaranteed for death and maturity claims. A bonus based on final performance at claim is a terminal bonus.

questions.question: What is a terminal bonus on a with-profits policy?
options: A bonus added every year that is guaranteed once declared
A penalty applied when the policy is surrendered early
A discretionary bonus that may be added when the policy becomes a claim, reflecting investment performance over its lifetime
A tax refund paid by Revenue at the end of the policy term
questions.explanation: A terminal (final) bonus is not guaranteed in advance; it is paid when the policy matures or a death claim arises and can make up a large part of the payout. It can be reduced or withdrawn if investment conditions are poor.

questions.question: What is meant by 'smoothing' in a with-profits fund?
options: Holding back some investment return in good years so that bonuses can be supported in poor years, reducing volatility in payouts
Spreading the premium evenly over the term of the policy
Averaging the unit price of the fund over the last 12 months before maturity
Charging an identical AMC to all policyholders
questions.explanation: The insurer declares bonuses that do not fully reflect short-term market movements, retaining reserves in good years to pay in bad years, so policy values move more gradually than the underlying assets.

questions.question: In which situation is a market value adjustment (MVA) most likely to be applied to a unitised with-profits policy?
options: On a death claim, to increase the amount paid to the estate
On a surrender when the value of the underlying assets is below the smoothed policy value
On every maturity claim, regardless of market conditions
When the insurer declares a higher reversionary bonus than the previous year
questions.explanation: An MVA reduces surrender or switch values when market values have fallen below the smoothed value, protecting remaining policyholders from those leaving taking more than their share. MVAs are typically not applied on death or on guaranteed dates such as maturity, per the policy terms.

questions.question: When does an endowment policy pay out its benefit?
options: Only on death during the term
Only on survival to the end of the term
On diagnosis of a specified serious illness
On the earlier of death during the term or survival to the end of the term
questions.explanation: An endowment combines savings and protection: it pays on maturity at the end of the term or on earlier death. Term assurance pays only on death; a pure endowment pays only on survival.

questions.question: Gráinne invested €50,000 in a five-year tracker bond offering 100% capital protection at maturity and 70% participation in the growth of a stock market index. At maturity the index is 20% lower than at the start. Assuming the guarantor meets its obligations, how much does she receive?
questions.explanation: With 100% capital protection she gets back her €50,000 when the index falls; participation applies only to growth. €40,000 and €43,000 wrongly apply the fall to her capital.

questions.question: Brian invests €50,000 in a tracker bond with 100% capital protection and 70% participation in index growth, measured from start to maturity with no averaging or cap. The index rises 40% over the term. Ignoring tax, what does he receive at maturity?
What is the main risk to the capital guarantee on a tracker bond?
options: A fall in the stock market index over the term
A change in the investor's attitude to risk
Inflation during the term of the bond
The failure of the bank or institution providing the guarantee (counterparty risk)
questions.explanation: The protection is usually provided by a third party, such as a bank issuing a deposit or note; if that counterparty fails, the capital may not be repaid in full. An index fall is exactly what the guarantee protects against.

questions.question: Lorcan wants to cash in a capital-protected tracker bond two years into a six-year term. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The capital protection usually applies only at maturity, so the early encashment value depends on the market value of the underlying instruments and may be less than he invested
He is entitled to his full capital back plus participation in index growth to date
Tracker bonds can never be encashed before maturity under any circumstances
The encashment value is guaranteed to equal his capital less a fixed 1% penalty
questions.explanation: Guarantees on tracker bonds apply on the maturity date. Before then the value reflects the current market price of the deposit/derivative structure, which can be below the original investment, and early exit charges may apply.

questions.question: A tracker bond measures index growth using the average of monthly index values over the final 12 months of the term. What is the effect of this averaging?
options: It guarantees a higher return than measuring the index on the maturity date
It removes counterparty risk from the bond
It can soften the impact of a sharp market fall just before maturity, but may reduce the return if the market rises strongly near the end
It increases the participation rate to 100%
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces the dependence on the index level on a single day: it helps if markets fall late in the term but dilutes gains if markets rise late. It does not affect the participation rate or counterparty risk.

questions.question: Rita, 68, sets up regular withdrawals of 5% a year from a €200,000 unit-linked bond to supplement her pension. Which statement is correct?
options: The withdrawals are guaranteed by the insurer for life
If the fund's growth after charges is less than 5% a year, the withdrawals will erode her capital
Withdrawals do not reduce the number of units in her policy
The withdrawals are treated as a return of capital and are always free of exit tax
questions.explanation: Withdrawals are met by cancelling units, so if net returns are below the withdrawal rate, the capital falls over time. Each withdrawal is a part surrender on which exit tax applies to the gain element.

questions.question: How are regular withdrawals from a unit-linked bond taken out after 1 January 2001 by an Irish-resident policyholder taxed?
options: Up to 5% a year can be withdrawn tax-free for 20 years, with tax deferred until final encashment
The withdrawals are taxed as income under PAYE
No tax applies to withdrawals until the eighth policy anniversary
Each withdrawal is a part surrender, and the insurer deducts exit tax on the gain element of the amount withdrawn
questions.explanation: A part surrender is a chargeable event under the gross roll-up regime, so exit tax is deducted on the portion of each withdrawal that represents gain. The '5% tax-deferred' rule is a UK concept and does not apply in Ireland.

questions.question: Seán, 35, wants to build a fund for his daughter's third-level education in 15 years. He can afford €300 a month, has an emergency fund already, and his attitude to risk is assessed as medium. Which is the most suitable recommendation?
options: A regular-premium unit-linked savings plan invested in a diversified multi-asset fund
A single-premium tracker bond funded by borrowing
A level term assurance policy for 15 years
A 12-month fixed-term deposit renewed annually, invested in a cash fund only
questions.explanation: He has a long horizon, regular disposable income and medium risk tolerance, which suit a regular-premium plan in a diversified fund. Term assurance has no savings element, and cash alone risks failing to beat inflation over 15 years.
questions.reference: Matching products to objectives and time horizon

questions.question: Mary, 70, has €60,000 on deposit. She will need €20,000 in 12 months to pay for a home extension. Where is the €20,000 most suitably held?
options: A five-year capital-protected tracker bond
A unit-linked equity fund bond
A deposit account
A with-profits bond with a market value adjustment
questions.explanation: Money needed in the short term should not be exposed to market falls, early encashment penalties or MVAs. A deposit account provides access and capital security for a known short-term need.

questions.question: Kevin's risk profile questionnaire indicates a high attitude to risk, but he tells his adviser that all of his €40,000 savings will be needed in two years for a house deposit. What should the adviser do?
options: Recommend a high-risk equity fund, as the stated attitude to risk must always be followed
Recommend a lower-risk option, because his short time horizon and limited capacity for loss outweigh his stated attitude to risk, and document the reasoning
Decline to give any advice, because the client's answers are inconsistent
Recommend a tracker bond with a five-year term, as capital is protected
questions.explanation: Suitability considers attitude to risk together with time horizon, objectives and capacity for loss. Here the short horizon and essential purpose of the money point to low risk; the adviser should explain and record why. A five-year bond does not match a two-year need.
questions.reference: Suitability: attitude to risk vs capacity for loss

questions.subtopic: Comparison with deposits and direct investment
questions.question: Compared with a unit-linked equity fund, which statement about a bank deposit account is correct?
options: It offers higher expected long-term returns
Its capital value moves daily with stock market prices
It is subject to the life assurance levy
It offers capital security, but there is a greater risk that returns will fall behind inflation over the long term
questions.explanation: Deposits protect the nominal capital (subject to the bank's solvency and the deposit guarantee scheme) but tend to deliver lower long-term returns, so inflation can erode their real value.

questions.subtopic: Comparison with deposits and direct investment
questions.question: Which is a valid reason for an investor to choose a unit-linked fund rather than buying shares directly?
options: It gives access to a diversified, professionally managed portfolio with a relatively small investment
Unit-linked funds guarantee that the capital invested will be returned
Gains in unit-linked funds are exempt from all Irish tax
Unit-linked funds always have lower charges than direct shareholdings
questions.explanation: Pooling allows modest sums to be spread across many assets and managed by professionals. Unit-linked funds carry no inherent guarantee, are subject to exit tax, and their charges can exceed those of direct holdings.

questions.question: Who legally owns the underlying assets of a unit-linked fund held under a life assurance policy?
options: The policyholders, in proportion to their units
The intermediary who arranged the policy
The life assurance company; policyholders have a contractual right to benefits measured by reference to their units
The Central Bank of Ireland, as custodian
questions.explanation: Units are a notional measure of entitlement under the policy; the assets belong to the life company, and the policyholder's rights are contractual. This is why the insurer's solvency and regulation matter to policyholders.

questions.question: Which is the main safeguard for unit-linked policyholders against the risk of an Irish life assurance company getting into financial difficulty?
options: The Insurance Compensation Fund pays 100% of the policy value
Prudential supervision by the Central Bank, including Solvency II capital requirements and the requirement to hold assets covering policyholder liabilities
The Deposit Guarantee Scheme covers up to €100,000 per policy
The State guarantees the value of all unit-linked funds
questions.explanation: Life policyholders rely mainly on prudential regulation: insurers must hold technical provisions backed by assets plus solvency capital. The Insurance Compensation Fund does not cover life assurance, and the Deposit Guarantee Scheme covers bank deposits, not life policies.

questions.question: Compared with a unit-linked fund, what is a key feature of a unitised with-profits fund?
options: The unit price falls and rises exactly in line with the underlying assets each day
There is no risk of any reduction on early surrender
The investor directly owns the underlying shares
Returns are smoothed through declared bonuses, so policy values are less volatile in the short term
questions.explanation: With-profits funds pass investment returns to policyholders through bonuses, with smoothing to reduce volatility. A surrender can still be reduced by an MVA, and the assets belong to the life company.

questions.question: For a chargeable event occurring in 2026 on a life assurance investment policy taken out after 1 January 2001 by an Irish-resident individual, what rate of exit tax applies?
questions.explanation: As of 2026, the exit tax rate on life assurance policies is 38%, reduced from 41% by Finance Act 2025 for events from 1 January 2026. Budget 2027 provides for a further reduction to 35% from 1 January 2027; 33% is the CGT rate in 2026.

questions.question: What is meant by the 'gross roll-up' regime for life assurance savings and investment policies?
options: Investment growth is taxed each year at the policyholder's marginal income tax rate
Premiums qualify for income tax relief at the marginal rate
Investment income and gains accumulate within the policy without annual tax, and tax is deducted by the insurer when a chargeable event occurs
Gains are taxed under CGT with the annual exemption available
questions.explanation: Under gross roll-up (policies from 1 January 2001), the fund grows free of tax, and the life company deducts exit tax on the gain when a chargeable event such as maturity, surrender or death happens.

questions.question: Philip invested €100,000 in a unit-linked bond in 2022. He fully surrenders it in June 2026 for €130,000. There have been no previous chargeable events or withdrawals. How much exit tax does the insurer deduct?
questions.explanation: Gain = €130,000 − €100,000 = €30,000. Exit tax at 38% (the 2026 rate, as of 2026) = €11,400, leaving net proceeds of €118,600. €12,300 uses the old 41% rate and €49,400 wrongly taxes the whole value.

questions.question: Budget 2027, announced in October 2026, provided for the exit tax rate on Irish life assurance policies to change from 1 January 2027. To what rate?
questions.explanation: As of 2026, Budget 2027 provides for life assurance exit tax to fall from 38% to 35% from 1 January 2027 (subject to the Finance Act). 31% is the reduced CGT rate announced in the same Budget.

questions.question: Sinéad's policy will mature in March 2027 with a gain of €20,000. Assuming the rate announced in Budget 2027 for chargeable events from 1 January 2027 is enacted, how much exit tax will be deducted?
questions.explanation: €20,000 × 35% = €7,000. €7,600 applies the 2026 rate of 38% and €8,200 the pre-2026 rate of 41%. The rates are as of 2026 announcements.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a chargeable event for exit tax on a gross roll-up life assurance policy?
options: Maturity of the policy
Switching from one fund to another within the same policy
Full surrender of the policy
Death of the life assured
questions.explanation: Chargeable events include maturity, surrender or part surrender, death, assignment and the eighth-anniversary deemed disposal. A switch between funds inside the policy is not a disposal of the policy, so no exit tax arises.

questions.question: Ger invested €100,000 in a unit-linked bond in March 2018. On the eighth anniversary in March 2026 the bond is worth €140,000. There have been no previous chargeable events or withdrawals. What exit tax arises on the anniversary?
options: Nothing, because exit tax applies only when money is actually withdrawn
questions.explanation: Every eighth anniversary is a deemed disposal. Gain = €140,000 − €100,000 = €40,000; at 38% (rate for 2026 events, as of 2026) the tax is €15,200, collected by the insurer cancelling units. €16,400 uses 41%; €53,200 taxes the whole value.

questions.question: Exit tax was deducted from Ann's bond on its eighth anniversary. She fully surrenders the bond two years later. Which statement is correct?
options: The full gain since outset is taxed again with no account taken of the earlier payment
Exit tax on the surrender takes account of the tax already paid on the deemed disposal, so the same gain is not taxed twice, and any overpayment can be refunded
No exit tax is due on the surrender, because a deemed disposal has already occurred
The earlier tax is refunded in full and the gain is instead charged to CGT
questions.explanation: Tax paid on a deemed disposal is effectively a payment on account: credit is given against tax on the later chargeable event, and if it exceeds the final liability (for example after a fall in value), the excess can be reclaimed.
questions.reference: Eight-year deemed disposal: credit for tax paid

questions.question: Who accounts to Revenue for exit tax on a chargeable event under an Irish life assurance policy held by an Irish-resident individual?
options: The life assurance company, which deducts the tax before paying the proceeds
The policyholder, through a self-assessment return
The intermediary who sold the policy
The policyholder's bank, when the proceeds are lodged
questions.explanation: The life company calculates the gain, deducts exit tax at source and pays it to Revenue. For an Irish policy the policyholder has no further tax to pay on that gain.
questions.reference: Exit tax: deduction by the insurer

questions.question: Dermot surrenders a gross roll-up life policy at a loss. As of 2026, which statement about the loss is correct?
options: It can be offset against his chargeable gains for CGT in the same year
It can be carried forward against future exit tax gains on his other policies
It cannot be offset against gains on other policies or against chargeable gains for CGT
It generates an income tax credit at the exit tax rate
questions.explanation: Exit tax is a final liability deducted at source, and losses on a life policy cannot be used against gains on other policies or for CGT purposes. Loss relief is not available under the regime.

questions.question: Which of the following assignments of a life assurance investment policy does NOT give rise to a chargeable event?
options: Assignment to an adult child as a gift
Sale of the policy to an unconnected third party
Assignment to a friend in exchange for cash
Assignment between spouses or civil partners
questions.explanation: Assignment is generally a chargeable event, but assignments between spouses or civil partners (including on separation or divorce) are excluded, so no exit tax arises at that point.

questions.question: In which situation will an Irish life company NOT deduct exit tax when a policy is surrendered at a gain?
options: The policyholder is over age 66
The policyholder is non-resident and has given the insurer the appropriate non-resident declaration
The policyholder pays income tax at the standard rate only
The gain is below €1,270
questions.explanation: Exit tax is not deducted where the policyholder is neither resident nor ordinarily resident and the required declaration is in place. Age, tax band and the CGT annual exemption (€1,270) do not affect exit tax.

questions.question: In outline, how were life assurance investment policies taken out before 1 January 2001 (the old basis) taxed?
options: Exit tax was deducted at 41% on every chargeable event
The policyholder paid CGT on the gain at encashment
Tax was paid by the life company within the fund on income and gains, and proceeds were generally paid without further tax to Irish-resident policyholders
Proceeds were taxed as income at the policyholder's marginal rate
questions.explanation: Under the old basis the life company was taxed on policyholder investment returns as they arose within the fund, so the proceeds were generally free of further tax for Irish residents. Gross roll-up and exit tax apply to policies from 2001.

questions.question: At what rate is the life assurance levy charged on premiums for Irish life assurance policies?
questions.explanation: As of 2026, a levy of 1% applies to life assurance premiums (Stamp Duties Consolidation Act 1999, s.124B). The 3% levy applies to non-life insurance premiums.

questions.question: Which type of business is excluded from the 1% life assurance levy?
options: Pension business
Single-premium investment bonds
Regular-premium savings plans
Term assurance policies
questions.explanation: Since Finance Act 2010, premiums for pension business and reinsurance are excluded from the levy. Investment bonds, savings plans and protection policies are within its scope (as of 2026).

questions.question: Maeve invests a single premium of €100,000 in a life assurance bond. The insurer deducts the 1% life assurance levy and allocates 100% of the balance, with no other charges. How much is invested in units?
questions.explanation: The levy is 1% of the premium: €100,000 × 1% = €1,000, leaving €99,000 to invest. €97,000 would apply the 3% non-life levy.

questions.question: How are the proceeds of a term assurance policy paid on the death of the life assured treated for tax purposes?
options: They are subject to exit tax on the full sum assured
They are free of income tax and CGT, but may be liable to CAT in the hands of the person who benefits
They are taxed as income of the deceased in the year of death
They are always completely tax-free, including for CAT
questions.explanation: Pure protection proceeds are not income or chargeable gains, and there is no investment gain for exit tax. However, the beneficiary may be liable to CAT unless an exemption applies or they paid the premiums themselves.

questions.question: Clodagh receives €150,000 from her own specified (serious) illness policy after a heart attack. She owns the policy and has always paid the premiums. How is the payment treated for tax?
options: It is taxed as income under PAYE
It is subject to exit tax at the current rate
It is a gift for CAT purposes
It is free of income tax and CGT, and as she paid her own premiums there is no CAT
questions.explanation: A serious illness lump sum paid to the life assured who owns the policy is not taxable income or a gain, and no gift arises because she funded the premiums herself.

questions.question: Darragh earns €60,000 a year and pays €1,200 a year for a Revenue-approved income protection policy. He pays tax at 40% on the top slice of his income. What is the net annual cost of the premium after tax relief?
questions.explanation: Relief is at the marginal rate on premiums up to 10% of total income (€6,000 here, so all €1,200 qualifies). Relief = €1,200 × 40% = €480, so net cost = €720. €960 assumes 20% relief.

questions.question: Fiona's total income for the year is €40,000. As of 2026, what is the maximum amount of income protection premiums for which she can claim tax relief in that year?
options: There is no limit
questions.explanation: Relief is available on premiums up to 10% of total income in the tax year: 10% × €40,000 = €4,000 (as of 2026, per Revenue).

questions.question: How are benefits paid under a personal income protection policy taxed?
options: They are tax-free, because the premiums were paid from taxed income
They are taxable as income, with tax deducted under PAYE
They are subject to exit tax at the insurer's rate
They are subject to CAT as a gift from the insurer
questions.explanation: Because premiums attract income tax relief, the replacement income is taxable; insurers typically deduct tax under the PAYE system before paying the benefit.

questions.question: As of 2026, what rate of Capital Acquisitions Tax applies to the taxable value of a gift or inheritance above the beneficiary's tax-free threshold?
questions.explanation: CAT is charged at 33% on the amount above the relevant group threshold; this rate has applied since December 2012 and was unchanged in Budget 2027.

questions.question: Gerard died in November 2026. His only child, Emma, inherits €500,000 from the proceeds of his own-life policy, which was not written in trust. She has received no previous gifts or inheritances. Ignoring any other reliefs, how much CAT is payable?
options: Nil, because life policy proceeds are exempt
questions.explanation: The Group A threshold for inheritances taken on or after 7 October 2026 is €420,000 (as of 2026, Budget 2027). Taxable = €500,000 − €420,000 = €80,000 × 33% = €26,400. €33,000 uses the previous €400,000 threshold.

questions.question: In November 2026, Aisling inherits €100,000 from her aunt's estate, funded by her aunt's life policy proceeds. She has received no previous gifts or inheritances. How much CAT is payable?
questions.explanation: A niece falls within Group B. For inheritances taken on or after 7 October 2026 the Group B threshold is €44,000 (as of 2026). Taxable = €100,000 − €44,000 = €56,000 × 33% = €18,480. €19,800 uses the old €40,000 threshold; €25,740 uses Group C.

questions.question: In November 2026, Tom inherits €50,000 from the estate of a close friend. He has received no previous gifts or inheritances. How much CAT is payable?
options: Nil
questions.explanation: A friend is in Group C. For inheritances taken on or after 7 October 2026 the Group C threshold is €22,000 (as of 2026). Taxable = €50,000 − €22,000 = €28,000 × 33% = €9,240. €9,900 uses the old €20,000 threshold.

questions.question: On 1 September 2026, Joe gives his son a gift of cash. What Group A threshold applies to this gift?
questions.explanation: The increase to €420,000 announced in Budget 2027 applies to gifts and inheritances taken on or after 7 October 2026. A gift taken on 1 September 2026 uses the €400,000 threshold that applied from 2 October 2024 (as of 2026).

questions.question: Michael dies and the €300,000 proceeds of his own-life policy pass under his will to his wife. What CAT is payable by his wife on the proceeds?
options: None, because inheritances between spouses are exempt from CAT
33% of the amount above the Group A threshold
33% of the amount above the Group C threshold
None, but only if the proceeds are reinvested in a Section 72 policy
questions.explanation: Gifts and inheritances between spouses and civil partners are fully exempt from CAT, whatever the amount.

questions.question: Liam and Orla live together but are not married or in a civil partnership. Liam has an own-life policy, not written in trust, and his will leaves the proceeds to Orla. He dies in November 2026. What is Orla's CAT position on the proceeds?
options: Exempt, because cohabitants are treated as spouses for CAT
Taxable, with the Group A threshold available
Taxable as an inheritance from Liam, with only the Group C threshold available
Exempt, because the proceeds of all life policies are exempt from CAT
questions.explanation: Cohabitants do not have the spouse exemption and fall within Group C (€22,000 for inheritances taken on or after 7 October 2026, as of 2026). Liam provided the premiums, so he is the disponer and the proceeds are an inheritance from him.

questions.question: Orla and Liam are an unmarried couple. Orla takes out a policy on Liam's life, owns the policy and pays all premiums from her own income. Liam dies and Orla receives €300,000. What is the CAT position?
options: Orla is taxed on the amount over the Group C threshold, as an inheritance from Liam
No CAT arises, because Orla provided the premiums and so did not take a benefit from Liam
Orla is taxed on the full €300,000 because no threshold applies to life policies
Liam's estate pays CAT on the proceeds before they are released to Orla
questions.explanation: With a life-of-another policy owned and funded by the beneficiary, the proceeds are her own property; there is no disponer other than herself, so no gift or inheritance arises. This is a standard planning solution for unmarried couples.

questions.question: For CAT purposes, who is generally regarded as the disponer in relation to the proceeds of a life assurance policy?
options: The life assurance company that pays the claim
The person whose life is insured, in every case
The beneficiary named in the policy
The person who provided the premiums
questions.explanation: The disponer is the person who provided the funds, so for a policy it is the person who paid the premiums. That is why the life-of-another arrangement, where the beneficiary pays, avoids a CAT charge.

questions.question: In 2026, Paddy gives his grandson a cash gift of €10,000. It is the only gift Paddy makes to him that year. As of 2026, how much of the gift counts towards the grandson's Group B lifetime threshold?
options: Nil
questions.explanation: The small gift exemption (€3,000 per disponer per beneficiary per calendar year, as of 2026) removes the first €3,000, so €7,000 is aggregated against the Group B threshold. The exemption applies to gifts only, not inheritances.

questions.question: Brenda pays €2,500 a year in premiums on a savings policy owned by her adult daughter. She makes no other gifts to her daughter. What is the CAT position on the premiums as of 2026?
options: The premiums are a gift but are covered by the small gift exemption, so nothing counts towards the daughter's threshold
The premiums are exempt because life assurance premiums can never be gifts
Each premium uses up the daughter's Group A threshold in full
CAT at 33% is payable on each premium
questions.explanation: Paying premiums on a policy owned by someone else is a gift to that person, but €2,500 a year is within the €3,000 annual small gift exemption (as of 2026), so no CAT and no use of the threshold.
questions.reference: CAT: premiums as gifts; small gift exemption

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Section 72 policy?
options: To pay exit tax on a maturing investment bond
To provide a tax-free lump sum on retirement
To pay inheritance tax arising on the insured's death, with the proceeds exempt from CAT to the extent used for that purpose
To fund the gift tax on lifetime gifts made after eight years
questions.explanation: A Section 72 (CATCA 2003) policy is effected by the insured expressly to pay 'relevant tax', mainly inheritance tax on their estate. Proceeds used to pay that tax are themselves exempt. Funding gift tax on lifetime gifts is the Section 73 purpose.

questions.question: Which of the following is a requirement for a policy to qualify under Section 72?
options: It must be a single-premium policy
Its proceeds must be payable no earlier than eight years after it is effected
It must be owned by the person who will inherit
Premiums must be paid by the insured, and the policy must be effected expressly to pay relevant tax
questions.explanation: A Section 72 policy must be a Revenue-approved policy effected by the insured, with premiums paid by the insured, expressly for paying relevant (inheritance) tax. The eight-year rule belongs to Section 73.

questions.question: Which set of conditions describes a Section 73 policy?
options: A whole-of-life policy on joint lives, paying out on the second death to fund inheritance tax
A single-premium bond held for at least five years, used to pay exit tax
A term policy paid for by the beneficiary, used to fund CGT on the sale of a business

Annual premiums paid for at least eight years, proceeds payable no earlier than eight years after the policy is effected, and used to pay gift tax on gifts made by the insured within one year after the appointed date
questions.explanation: Section 73 policies fund tax on lifetime (inter vivos) gifts. The appointed date must be at least eight years after the policy starts, premiums are paid annually for at least eight years, and the proceeds cover tax on gifts made within one year after that date. Proceeds not used for that tax are treated as a gift.

questions.question: The proceeds of Seamus's Section 72 policy are €400,000, but the inheritance tax due on his estate is only €250,000. What is the position on the excess €150,000?
options: It is exempt from CAT, like the rest of the proceeds
It must be returned to the life company
It is subject to exit tax at the current rate
It is not covered by the exemption and is treated as an inheritance subject to CAT in the normal way
questions.explanation: The Section 72 exemption applies only to the extent the proceeds are used to pay relevant tax. Any surplus passes as an inheritance and is liable to CAT if it exceeds the beneficiaries' thresholds.

questions.question: Why is a Section 72 policy for a married couple usually set up on a joint-lives, second-death basis?
options: Because the spouse exemption usually means little or no inheritance tax arises on the first death; the liability arises when the survivor dies and assets pass to the children
Because Section 72 policies can only be written on two lives
Because the premiums are then eligible for income tax relief
Because second-death policies are exempt from the life assurance levy
questions.explanation: Assets passing between spouses are CAT-exempt, so the main inheritance tax bill for the children typically comes on the second death. A joint-life, second-death policy matches the cover to that liability and is usually cheaper.

questions.question: Why might a parent write an own-life protection policy in trust for their children?
options: To make the proceeds exempt from CAT in all cases
To obtain income tax relief on the premiums
So that the proceeds are paid to the trustees for the children without forming part of the estate or waiting for a grant of probate
To convert the policy into a Section 73 policy
questions.explanation: A trust directs the proceeds outside the estate, so they can be paid quickly to the intended beneficiaries. CAT may still apply to the children, because the parent paid the premiums.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of underwriting a life assurance proposal?
options: To calculate the commission payable to the intermediary
To decide which investment fund the premium is invested in
To assess the risk presented by the applicant and decide whether, and on what terms, to accept it
To check that the applicant has made a will
questions.explanation: Underwriting assesses the risk of a claim so the insurer can decide whether to accept the proposal and at what premium and terms, keeping premiums fair across policyholders.

questions.question: In life assurance, anti-selection (adverse selection) refers to:
options: The tendency of people who know they are higher risk to seek cover, or more cover, than average
An insurer's refusal to insure smokers
The insured behaving more carelessly once insured
A policyholder choosing a fund with low risk
questions.explanation: Anti-selection occurs when applicants with greater knowledge of their own higher risk are more likely to apply for cover. Underwriting aims to identify and price such risks.

questions.question: Which situation is the clearest example of moral hazard in protection insurance?
options: An applicant with a family history of heart disease applying for life cover
A smoker paying higher premiums
An insurer passing part of a large risk to a reinsurer
A person whose income protection benefit would exceed their take-home pay having less incentive to return to work
questions.explanation: Moral hazard relates to the insured's behaviour or attitude changing because they are insured. Over-insurance on income protection is a classic example, which is why benefits are limited relative to earnings.

questions.question: What is the role of the proposal (application) form in life assurance?
options: It sets out the investment performance of the policy
It records the applicant's answers to the insurer's questions, which the insurer relies on to assess the risk
It is the policy document issued after acceptance
It is a claim form completed by the beneficiary
questions.explanation: The proposal form gathers information about the applicant's health, lifestyle, occupation and finances. The insurer relies on these answers when underwriting and setting terms.

questions.question: Under the traditional common law position, before the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019 applied, what was the applicant's duty of disclosure?
options: A duty to answer only the questions asked, with reasonable care
No duty of disclosure; it was up to the insurer to find out the facts
A duty of utmost good faith to disclose all material facts, whether or not the insurer asked about them
A duty to disclose only facts known to their GP
questions.explanation: Insurance was a contract of utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei): the proposer had to volunteer all material facts, and non-disclosure could allow the insurer to avoid the policy from the start.

questions.question: Under section 8 of the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, what is a consumer's pre-contractual duty when applying for a life policy?
options: To volunteer every fact that a prudent insurer would consider material
To answer the insurer's specific questions honestly and with reasonable care, with no duty to volunteer further information
To obtain a medical report at their own expense
To answer only those questions that relate to smoking
questions.explanation: Section 8 replaces the duty of utmost good faith and voluntary disclosure for consumers: the consumer must answer the insurer's specific questions honestly and with reasonable care, and is not required to volunteer anything beyond them.

questions.question: From what date did the pre-contractual disclosure provisions in section 8 of the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019 come into effect?
options: 1 September 2021
1 January 2019
1 September 2020
1 January 2023
questions.explanation: Most of the Act commenced on 1 September 2020, but sections 8, 9, 12 and 14(1)-(5), including the pre-contractual disclosure and misrepresentation remedy provisions, were deferred to 1 September 2021.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, how must an insurer frame the questions it relies on for disclosure?
options: As a single general question asking for anything else the insurer should know
Verbally only, so that the consumer can ask for clarification
In whatever form the insurer chooses, provided the consumer signs a declaration
As specific questions in plain and intelligible language, on paper or another durable medium
questions.explanation: The Act requires specific (not general) questions in plain, intelligible language on paper or another durable medium. A catch-all question cannot be used to place a wider disclosure duty on the consumer.

questions.question: A question on a proposal form governed by the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019 is ambiguous, and the consumer honestly interprets it in a reasonable way that leads them to answer 'no'. How is the ambiguity treated?
options: It is resolved in favour of the insurer, as the drafter of the form
It is resolved in favour of the consumer
The policy is automatically void
The intermediary becomes liable for any claim
questions.explanation: The Act provides that any ambiguity in the insurer's questions is resolved in the consumer's favour, placing responsibility for clear questions on the insurer.

questions.question: An applicant leaves a question about hospital admissions blank, and the insurer issues the policy without following it up. Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, assuming there was no fraud, what is the effect?
options: The insurer can later avoid the policy for non-disclosure of any hospital admissions
The consumer must pay a penalty before any claim is paid
The insurer is treated as having waived its right to that information
The policy cannot come into force until the answer is supplied
questions.explanation: Where an insurer fails to follow up an absent or obviously incomplete answer, it is deemed to have waived further disclosure on that point, unless there was fraudulent, intentional or reckless concealment.
