questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, a consumer answered all questions honestly and with reasonable care, but one answer later proves to be inaccurate (an innocent misrepresentation). What may the insurer do when a claim arises?
options: Avoid the policy and return the premiums
Reduce the claim in proportion to the extra premium it would have charged
Refuse the claim but keep the premiums
Pay the claim; it cannot avoid the contract for the misrepresentation
questions.explanation: Where the misrepresentation was neither negligent nor fraudulent, the insurer must pay the claim and is not entitled to avoid the contract because of it.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, a consumer negligently failed to disclose a condition. The insurer shows it would have accepted the risk but charged €75 a month instead of the €50 a month actually charged. On a €300,000 death claim, what is the insurer entitled to pay?
options: Nothing, with premiums refunded
questions.explanation: For negligent misrepresentation where a higher premium would have been charged, the claim may be reduced proportionately: €50 / €75 x €300,000 = €200,000. €150,000 wrongly reduces by the €25 difference as a share of the premium charged (50%).
questions.reference: Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, s.9 - proportionate remedy

questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, a consumer negligently misrepresented their health, and the insurer proves it would not have offered cover on any terms had it known the facts. What remedy is available?
options: The insurer may avoid the contract and refuse claims, but must return the premiums paid
The insurer must pay the claim in full
The insurer may pay half the claim
The insurer may avoid the contract and keep all premiums
questions.explanation: The remedy for negligent misrepresentation reflects what the insurer would have done: if it would not have contracted at all, it may avoid the contract and refuse claims, but must return the premiums.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, Paul negligently failed to mention past knee surgery when applying for income protection. The insurer would have issued the policy at the same premium but with an exclusion for knee conditions. Paul now claims for a heart condition. What is the likely outcome?
options: The insurer may avoid the policy entirely
The claim is reduced proportionately
The contract is treated as including the knee exclusion, so the heart claim is assessed normally
The claim is refused because any negligent misrepresentation voids the policy
questions.explanation: Where the insurer would have contracted on different terms (other than premium), the contract can be treated as if those terms applied. A knee exclusion does not affect a heart claim, so that claim is assessed on its merits.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, what remedy does the insurer have where a consumer's pre-contract misrepresentation was fraudulent?
options: It may only reduce the claim proportionately
It may avoid the contract
It must pay the claim but may increase future premiums
It has no remedy if the policy has been in force for over a year
questions.explanation: For fraudulent misrepresentation the insurer may avoid the contract. Proportionate remedies apply only to negligent misrepresentation.

questions.question: In life underwriting, what is a PMAR?
options: A Private Medical Attendant's Report obtained from the applicant's own doctor
A Proposal Management and Acceptance Record
A premium adjustment for male applicants
A policy maturity and renewal notice
questions.explanation: A PMAR is a report from the applicant's GP or other treating doctor about their medical history. It is requested with the applicant's consent where the proposal answers or sum assured make it necessary.

questions.question: What are non-medical limits in life underwriting?
options: The maximum sum assured an insurer will ever offer
Limits on the number of claims a policyholder can make
Levels of cover, by age, up to which an insurer will normally accept a proposal without routine medical evidence if the proposal answers are clear
The ages above which no cover is available
questions.explanation: Within non-medical limits, a clean proposal can be accepted on the answers alone. Above them, insurers routinely ask for evidence such as a PMAR, medical exam or blood tests, with limits falling as age rises.

questions.question: What is tele-underwriting?
options: Underwriting carried out entirely by an automated website with no questions
Medical and lifestyle questions asked by telephone by a trained interviewer, often a nurse, on behalf of the insurer
Use of a smartphone app to track the applicant's exercise
Underwriting carried out by the applicant's GP over the telephone
questions.explanation: Tele-underwriting gathers medical and lifestyle information by telephone interview, which can be faster than paper forms and may reduce the need for GP reports.

questions.question: Gerry, earning €35,000 a year with no dependants or debts, applies for €3 million of life cover. Which type of underwriting is most relevant to the insurer's concern?
options: Medical underwriting of his blood pressure
Occupational underwriting of his job
Genetic underwriting
Financial underwriting, to check that the cover is justified by his financial circumstances
questions.explanation: Financial underwriting checks that the sum assured is reasonable for the client's income, debts and needs, guarding against over-insurance and the anti-selection or moral hazard it may indicate.

questions.question: An applicant presents a normal level of risk for their age and smoker status. What underwriting outcome is most likely?
options: Acceptance at standard rates
Acceptance with a premium loading
Postponement
Decline
questions.explanation: Most applicants are accepted at standard rates, meaning the normal premium for their age, smoker status, term and sum assured.

questions.question: Clodagh has well-controlled high blood pressure. The insurer offers life cover at its normal rate plus 50%. What is this outcome called?
options: An exclusion
A postponement
A premium loading
A decline
questions.explanation: A loading is an extra premium charged where the risk is higher than standard, often expressed as a percentage of the standard premium or a fixed amount per €1,000 sum assured.

questions.question: Fergal, a plasterer with a history of recurring back problems, applies for income protection. Which underwriting decision is most typical?
options: Decline all cover permanently
Accept at standard rates with no special terms
Postpone until he retires
Accept with an exclusion for back conditions
questions.explanation: Exclusions are commonly used for income protection and serious illness cover where a specific pre-existing condition gives a higher risk, allowing the rest of the risk to be covered at normal terms.

questions.question: Niamh applies for life cover while awaiting the results of investigations into a recently found lump. What is the insurer most likely to do?
options: Postpone a decision until the investigations are complete and the outcome is known
Accept immediately at standard rates
Accept with an exclusion for all cancers for life
Decline permanently
questions.explanation: Where the risk cannot be assessed until test results or recovery are known, insurers usually postpone and ask the applicant to reapply later.

questions.question: Under Part 4 of the Disability Act 2005, what is the position on genetic test information in life assurance underwriting in Ireland?
options: Insurers may require a genetic test for cover over €500,000
Insurers may use favourable results but not unfavourable ones
Genetic data may not be processed for the purposes of a policy of insurance or life assurance
Applicants must disclose any genetic test they have taken
questions.explanation: Section 42 of the Disability Act 2005 prohibits processing genetic data in relation to insurance and life assurance (among other purposes), so insurers cannot require tests or use their results.

questions.question: Under the Insurance Ireland Code of Practice on underwriting mortgage protection for cancer survivors that took effect in December 2023, how long after the end of treatment (for someone diagnosed as an adult) will participating insurers disregard a cancer diagnosis, subject to the Code's conditions and cover limit?
options: 2 years
7 years
10 years
15 years
questions.explanation: The Code provides that a cancer diagnosis is disregarded for mortgage protection where treatment ended more than 7 years before the application (5 years if diagnosed under 18), for cover up to €500,000. Check whether this has since been placed on a statutory footing.
questions.reference: Insurance Ireland Code of Practice (2023) - right to be forgotten

questions.question: Why does a life insurer use reinsurance?
options: To pass part of its risk, especially on large or unusual cases, to another insurer in return for a share of the premium
To provide investment returns to policyholders
To avoid having to underwrite any proposals
To insure the intermediary against complaints
questions.explanation: Reinsurance spreads risk, protects the insurer against large or concentrated claims and allows it to accept larger cases. Reinsurers also provide underwriting guidance.

questions.question: Which document is essential to support any death claim on a life policy?
options: The deceased's latest payslip
A copy of the deceased's tax return
A death certificate
A medical report from a consultant
questions.explanation: Proof of death, normally a death certificate, is required for every death claim, together with proof of title to the proceeds and usually the policy document.

questions.question: Martin owned a policy on his own life, not in trust and not assigned. He has died leaving a will. To whom will the insurer pay the proceeds?
options: Directly to his spouse on production of the death certificate
To the executors of his estate once they produce a grant of probate
To his eldest child
To the Revenue Commissioners pending tax clearance
questions.explanation: An own-life policy not in trust or assigned forms part of the deceased's estate, so the insurer pays the legal personal representatives, who must prove their title with a grant of representation (probate where there is a will).

questions.question: Assuming no other legal complications, why can proceeds of a policy written under trust usually be paid faster than proceeds payable to an estate?
options: Because trust policies do not require a death certificate
Because trust proceeds are tax-free in all cases
Because the trustees can claim with the death certificate and trust documents without waiting for a grant of representation
Because the insurer pays trust claims before investigating
questions.explanation: The trustees have legal title to the policy, so they can claim on production of the death certificate and proof of their title, without the delay of obtaining probate or letters of administration.

questions.question: Áine's life policy was assigned to her mortgage lender as security. She dies owing €180,000 and the policy pays €250,000. Assuming no other claims, how are the proceeds dealt with?
options: €180,000 goes to the lender to clear the loan and the €70,000 balance goes to her estate
The full €250,000 is paid to her estate
The full €250,000 is kept by the lender
The proceeds are split equally between the lender and her estate
questions.explanation: As assignee by way of security, the lender is entitled to the amount needed to clear the debt (€180,000). The surplus, €250,000 - €180,000 = €70,000, is returned for the benefit of her estate.

questions.question: What evidence is generally needed to support a serious illness claim?
options: A death certificate
Confirmation from the claimant's employer that they are off work
A note from a pharmacist
Medical evidence, usually from a consultant or specialist, that the diagnosis meets the policy definition
questions.explanation: Insurers assess serious illness claims against strict policy definitions, so they need specialist medical evidence of the diagnosis and its severity. Inability to work is irrelevant for this cover.

questions.question: For an income protection claim to be paid, which of the following must normally be shown?
options: That the claimant has been diagnosed with cancer, heart attack or stroke
That the claimant has been continuously unable to work, as defined in the policy, throughout the deferred period, with supporting medical evidence and proof of earnings
That the claimant has been off work for at least one day
That the claimant has a terminal illness
questions.explanation: Income protection claims require medical evidence of incapacity under the policy's definition throughout the deferred period, and evidence of pre-claim earnings to calculate the benefit.

questions.question: Ruairí claims on his serious illness policy after a mild heart attack. The insurer declines the main claim. Assuming full disclosure, what is the most likely reason?
options: The cardiac event did not meet the severity criteria in the policy's heart attack definition
Heart attacks are never covered by serious illness policies
He was still able to go back to work
He did not make a will
questions.explanation: Claims are assessed against precise definitions, and some cardiac events do not meet the required severity. Ability to work is not relevant to serious illness cover; some policies may offer a partial payment in such cases.

questions.question: Orlaith stopped paying premiums on her term policy and the grace period has passed without payment. Two months later she dies. What is the likely position?
options: The full sum assured is payable because she was insured when she stopped paying
Half the sum assured is payable
The policy's cash value is payable
No claim is payable because the policy had lapsed
questions.explanation: Once the grace period passes without payment, a term policy lapses and cover ends. Term policies have no cash value, so nothing is payable.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, a consumer notifies a claim later than the policy conditions require. When may the insurer refuse the claim because of the late notification?
options: Always, because the policy condition was breached
Only where the insurer has been prejudiced by the late notification
Never, because the Act abolished all notification conditions
Only if the delay was more than 7 days
questions.explanation: The Act provides that late notification of a claim does not entitle the insurer to refuse it unless the insurer has been prejudiced by the delay.

questions.question: Under the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019, if a consumer makes a fraudulent claim, what may the insurer do?
options: Only reduce the fraudulent claim proportionately
Refuse the claim, terminate the contract and also recover all claims paid in the past
Refuse the claim and terminate the contract, but earlier valid claims are not affected
Pay the claim but increase future premiums
questions.explanation: Section 18 allows the insurer to refuse a fraudulent claim and terminate the contract, but a valid claim made earlier under the same policy is not affected by a later fraudulent claim.

questions.question: Under the GDPR, how is health information collected during underwriting and claims classified?
options: As special category personal data, requiring additional safeguards and a specific lawful basis such as explicit consent
As public data that may be shared freely with other insurers
As ordinary personal data with no additional protections
As anonymous data, because it relates to medical matters
questions.explanation: Data concerning health is special category data under the GDPR. Insurers must have a lawful basis and an additional condition, such as explicit consent, to process it, and must keep it secure and use it only for stated purposes.
questions.reference: GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018 - special category data

questions.question: Why do insurers typically look more closely at the original application when a death or illness claim arises in the first year or two of a policy?
options: Because early claims are never payable
Because early claims carry a higher risk that relevant information was not disclosed accurately at application
Because early claims are always paid in instalments
Because the cooling-off period extends to two years
questions.explanation: Claims soon after inception are more likely to involve pre-existing conditions, so insurers check the answers given at application against medical records. Any remedy must still follow the Consumer Insurance Contracts Act 2019 rules.
